entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
This course includes the following topic(s): Econ/Civics: Grade 11 (Canada), Ethics: Part 5, Current Events: Grades 9-12, Community Read Alouds: Grades 1-12

About Econ/Civics: Grade 11 (Canada)
This course covers a variety of citizenship topics. Students spend the first term learning the art of asking questions as a means of relationship building. The second term focuses on government as students explore topics of government through a historical survey of Canada's Prime Ministers. The year finishes with a term of economics where students learn a variety of economic theories.

About Ethics: Part 5
Students will explore characteristics shared by all Image-Bearers and learn how to guard against good servants becoming bad masters by continuing Charlotte Mason's text written directly to students. Students finish Book II in this course.

About Current Events: Grades 9-12
Students are exposed to current events by reading from a variety of sources and having conversations with teachers. Topics such as scientific discoveries, the arts, and human interest stories are generally suitable.

About Community Read Alouds: Grades 1-12
This is meant to be a read-aloud for all ages to enjoy together in the afternoon at least 1 time a week. We encourage you to choose a book that is specific to your region. However, we will offer some suggestions in the Grades 1-3 Literature lessons and Grades 4+ Citizenship lessons. The suggested book titles will be available June 1st in the lesson plans.

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content:
Econ/Civics: Grade 11 (Canada)
Lessons are occasionally integrated with composition lessons.
The book The Prime Ministers: Canada's Leaders and the Nation They Shaped will be read over two years (Grades 10 and 11). However, since this is the first year this book will be used, Grades 10 and 11 will have the same readings in 2026-2027.

Ethics: Part 5
Ourselves by Charlotte Mason is scheduled over five years. In a multi-age context, students can jump into the book wherever the class is reading. Otherwise, students should begin the book in Part 1.

blocks.text: If you, the student, are learning at home, work to schedule a time with your teacher when you can complete the lessons from Ourselves or your Ethics reading together, as these lessons are much richer when shared and discussed.
Connect back to the previous lesson. (Optional for Current Events).
For news sources: Scan the headlines first to get an overview, and then choose a story to read.

Read the selection assigned or the news story chosen for the time assigned. For rich, dense, or more challenging books such as Ourselves, it is a good idea to read them aloud. Keep an eye out for quotes to put in your commonplace book or events or characters to put down in your Book of Centuries.

Process and integrate your reading by narrating either orally or in writing. Some lesson plans will give you a suggestion of how best to narrate. To keep yourself on track, you might want to set a timer so you stop reading with enough time to narrate.

After your narration, think about how what you read connects to other subjects, other books, other things you've read or watched, or seen in the past or present. For current events, look up where events occurred on a map and ask questions together to discern the quality of the piece. (e.g., Are there sources cited? Is there an obvious bias? If so, what do other authors have to say on this subject? Are arguments supported by evidence? Is that evidence credible?) Consider reading an alternative perspective.
Record important ideas in your Citizenship Notebooks. Make a calendar of current events.

These lessons are written directly to students, but to assist them throughout the year, please read through this section and the lesson plans so you are familiar with the instructions and flow of the lessons. You may also want to preview and choose which news sites to offer students.

Those educating at home might pick one lesson to read aloud (such as the Ethics readings on Cultural Engagement, Conscience, etc.) with their students to keep up the habit of oral narration and foster conversation and relationship and then simply give students these lesson plans and the rest of the books and check in with them throughout the term for conversation, support, and accountability. 

It is valuable for those in a classroom setting to also have a mix of lessons, which students complete themselves silently, and others read aloud and narrated together. Classroom settings lend themselves well to additional discussion and sharing at the end of lessons, after everyone has narrated either together or independently in writing.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 11 (Canada) - Lesson 13
lessons.body:
The Prime Ministers' Introduction and Sir John A. Macdonald
⍞ Materials: The Prime Ministers

➜ INTRO
In his Introduction, J. D. M. Stewart recalls speaking to a group of high school students who could not recognize one of Canada's most well-known past Prime Ministers. How many can you name? What do you know about their time in office?
Stewart writes that if "we want to understand the country, it is imperative that we understand those who led it." This term, you will read the first half of his book The Prime Ministers, covering the years 1867-1963: nearly a century of Prime Ministers from John A. Macdonald to John Diefenbaker.

➜ ANNOTATE
As your ability to read higher-level books in high school grows, it is helpful to learn new ways to interact with the text while you are reading to help you grasp what the author is saying. Non-fiction books are usually good candidates for annotating while you read. Maybe you want to underline the main ideas or interesting points. Maybe you want to put a question mark in the margin if something is unclear. Think about how to help yourself engage with the information in the book to make it your own. Recall what you learned in the previous term from How to Mark a Book. 

∞ Article Link: How to Mark a Book by Mortimer Adler

Experiment with different ways to do that. Some students do best by recording themselves talking about the reading, while others may need to discuss the material with another person. Whatever you do, your annotations should help you to further solidify the main points or ideas in your mind. Write down any questions, comments, or connections that arise from your review of your annotations after reading. Try different ways and discuss your observations about what works well and what doesn't with your teacher.

Explore ways that might be most helpful for you as you read each week. Advances in technology make many more annotation options available to serve us and our various ways of processing. Some might do great with a pencil and a book, while others might benefit from colors, Post-its, or speech-to-text options.

For today, if you are new to this, start simply by putting a mark in the margin or a Post-it flag when you come across a main idea or an important point the author is making. For others who have been doing this already, see what new ways you might want to experiment with this term.

While reading The Prime Ministers, strive to make connections to ideas, events, and people you have come across in previous readings you have done. Each chapter gives a window into the period of Canada's history during which the particular Prime Minister served. They often faced similar issues, but addressed them quite differently.

As you read, also make notes of historical figures and events that are unfamiliar to you, and do further research on what interests you.

➜ READ
p.ix-xi "A small anecdote illustrates" - "is to know ourselves."
p.1-12 "Sir John A. Macdonald" - "principal Father of Confederation."
• What were some of the major issues Macdonald addressed in his first term as Prime Minister?

➜ VIEW
With each new Prime Minister you learn about, look at their portrait reproduced in the photo pages between p. 180 and 181.

➜ NARRATE
Narrate in a way that helps you interact with the ideas in the reading. For some, that might be narrating orally or silently to yourself, in writing, by drawing a map, a diagram, or a picture, writing a diary/letter from the point of view of one of the historical figures, describing what happened, or writing a bulleted list of points and questions. For others, it might be helpful to make marks in the book as you read and then narrate as you look at what you marked in the chapter. Experiment and see what works well for you, and you can vary your approach week to week.

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: What Would Keynes Do?, link, and notebook

➜ NOTE
Part 2 lessons cover Ch.5, sections of Ch.3, and Ch.4.

➜INTRO
Skim back over the sections to remind yourself of the topics from Part 1; remember that you encountered several economists and their approaches/positions on the specific issue being covered. Focus on theory and positions rather than trying to memorize names. 

• DEFINITIONS:
The marginal tax rate is the amount of additional tax paid for every additional dollar earned as income. The average tax rate is the total tax paid divided by the total income earned. If you want to know more, see the expanded definition from TaxEDU.

➜ VIEW
∞ Link: Marginal Tax Rate (TaxEDU)

➜ RECAP        
Opportunity cost = the next best alternative you forgo (p.45)

Deadweight welfare = money spent is greater than utility gained, leading to an inefficient allocation of resources (p.71)

Income effect = higher wages mean we can gain our target income through working less and enjoying more leisure time (p.93)

➜ READ 
p.150-157

➜ DISCUSS and/or WRITE
• "There is no such thing as a tax cut without an opportunity cost" (p.153).  If discussing these lessons with someone is not an option, write down your thoughts about the quote.
lessons.teacherNotes:
TEACHER TIP:

• COMPOSITION
Write an essay on the economic positions of "sweatshops." Be sure to include your position and support your answer with the text and/or other sources.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 11 (Canada) - Lesson 31
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: What Would Keynes Do?, link, and notebook

• DEFINITIONS:
Libertarianism - a political philosophy that strongly values individual freedom and minimal government involvement

Welfare state - a concept of government in which the state plays a key role in the economic and social well-being of its citizens

➜ RECAP        
GDP = Gross Domestic Product, the national income of a country (p.78).

➜ READ
p.99-102

➜ DISCUSS and/ or WRITE
• Discuss the charts on p.101 as they relate to immigration and supply and demand for labor.

➜ INTRO
Entrepreneurship is essential to the economy. Two twentieth-century economists, Joseph Schumpeter and Israel Kirzner, contribute more to the conversation. In Chapter 2, you read how Kirzner suggests that entrepreneurs (and consumers) find ways around problems (p.55), and Schumpeter talks about creative destruction (p.158) - more on that in the finance section. Innovation brings about change, and entrepreneurs are change agents. 

In the non-profit sector, innovation is about supporting a mission-driven vision that provides a product or service to supply a need. Think about this in the context of social needs or religious ministry; the organizations that support these areas can be for-profit or non-profit. Non-profit organizations also have business structures. Since the lesson discusses the idea of being employed by a business vs. setting up your own business, now is a good time to take a quick look at what that might mean for an entrepreneur in the ministry sector. Let's take a look at basic finance for nonprofits by watching a short video as an introduction to accounting and business practices.

➜ READ
p.104-107 

➜ DISCUSS and/or WRITE
• Discuss the idea of self-employment. Write a brief pro/con list for working for a company vs. being your own boss. What are the "trade-offs"?

➜ VIEW
Watch the section on non-profit accounting. This is a short clip made for a specific software platform, but the fundamental ideas are all explained well.
∞ Video Link: What is Accounting? (Aplos)
